paras: The attack on the home of Andrew Cheney was a midnight attempt in October 1903 by white men to break into the house of Cheney, a Black farmer near Americus, Georgia, and capture him after a quarrel with a white neighbor. Cheney fired on the attackers, badly wounding a white farmer, John Suggs, and the party withdrew. Cheney surrendered to the sheriff and asked for protection; the case drew wire coverage across the South, some of it headlined as a Black man shooting a "whitecap."

Cheney farmed in the Fifteenth district below Americus, in Sumter County. By his own account he had a "slight difficulty" on Saturday, October 10, with Walter Bray, a young white farmer, and he believed the later attack was meant to punish him for it. The Americus Times-Recorder relayed a fuller story told in town: Cheney's wagon ran into Bray's buggy on the road, and in the fight that followed Bray used a rail and Cheney a knife, leaving Bray cut on the arm.

Several hours later, around midnight, an "avenging posse" of four or five young men, described as well known in the area, came to Cheney's house, where he had barricaded himself. According to Cheney's statement, the men demanded that he open the door, and when he refused they tried to batter it down in order to capture him. He fired point blank at the party, and the bullet struck John Suggs, a young white farmer, through the left lung, after which the others left.
The local paper added that some thought the shots came from a confederate of Cheney's outside the house, a theory no later report repeated.

On Monday, October 12, Cheney surrendered to Sheriff Bell, admitted the shooting and asked for protection. He was held in the Americus jail "for safe keeping, pending a full and complete investigation," and the Times-Recorder noted that he did not care to leave it. Suggs, first said to be at the point of death, was reported improving on October 14 and entirely out of danger by October 20.

The Times-Recorder expected nothing to be done until the grand jury investigated "the shooting and other features of the affair." No report of a grand jury finding, a charge against anyone, or Cheney's release appears in the coverage.

Most papers ran an Americus dispatch of October 12 that rested on Cheney's statement and called it "the only story of the tragedy received thus far." Headlines on the same text differed sharply: the Savannah Morning News ran "Attack on Negro May Lead to Death," while the Birmingham Age-Herald ran "Negro Confesses Guilt" above Cheney's account that he had fired in defense. The local Times-Recorder, under "Bullets Fired at Pursuers," called the attackers an "avenging posse," added the rival theory about a confederate, and cautioned that "there may be other versions of the whole affair."

Reprints carried the story further afield under the label of whitecapping: the Union Times in South Carolina and the Ocala Banner in Florida headlined it "Negro Shoots Whitecap" on October 16, and the Dawson News in Georgia ran "White-Cappers in Sumter" on October 21. These reprints still described Suggs as dying or badly wounded, days after the Americus paper reported him recovering. The Marietta Journal reduced the case to one line, noting Cheney's claim that Suggs "was with a mob which attacked his home."

A Vermont Watchman editorial of October 22, its opening lost, told what appears to be the same case without names: a whipping party "attired as white caps" left "carrying with them three badly wounded comrades," and "the negro's door was still on its hinges." No coverage of the episode in the Black press was found.

Accounts differ on the earlier quarrel, which Cheney called slight but the local paper described as a road fight with a rail and a knife. On the wounded, the wire named only Suggs, the Times-Recorder added Bray's cut from the road fight, and the Vermont editorial spoke of three, which the local reports do not support. Only the Vermont editorial says the attackers were disguised or meant to whip Cheney; in the Georgia reports they sought to "capture" him and "inflict punishment" for the quarrel.

reader.title: Attack on the home of Andrew Cheney
bases: A party of four or five white men tried at midnight to break into a Black farmer's house to capture or punish him after a quarrel, and was driven off when he fired (A2, A3); several headlines called the attackers whitecaps (A6, A9), but no organized band is described.

No one was killed: Cheney was not harmed in the attack and the wounded white man, Suggs, recovered (A4, A8). The party of four or five private citizens acted without authority to 'inflict punishment' for Cheney's quarrel with Bray (A2, A3), so this was at most an attempted extralegal punishment, and no paper reports a threat to kill.

The local Americus paper (A2) and the Americus wire (A1, A3) agree that a party of white men attacked Cheney's house at night and that Suggs was shot, though details of the attack rest largely on Cheney's own statement (A3, A4) and the local paper reports a rival theory about who fired (A2).

accounts.gist: A posse of white men tried at midnight to batter down his door to capture him; he refused to open it and fired point blank, wounding Suggs, and the rest left. He thought they meant to punish him for a slight difficulty with Bray.

accounts.label: Americus Times-Recorder (local reports)
accounts.gist: Cheney's wagon ran into Bray's buggy, and in the road fight Bray used a rail and Cheney a knife; hours later an 'avenging posse' of four or five young men attacked his barricaded house. Some thought a confederate of Cheney outside fired the shots.

accounts.label: Vermont Watchman editorial
accounts.gist: After a quarrel, a white neighbor persuaded friends to whip a Black farmer; dressed as white caps they tried to batter his door and left carrying three badly wounded comrades.

framing.detail: The Age-Herald headlined the wire 'Negro Confesses Guilt' while printing Cheney's account that he fired in defense against a posse.

The Americus Times-Recorder ('Bullets Fired at Pursuers') called the attackers an 'avenging posse', reported a theory that a confederate fired, and allowed 'there may be other versions'; follow-ups tracked Suggs's recovery and Cheney's custody.
The Savannah Morning News headlined 'Attack on Negro May Lead to Death' and noted Cheney's was 'the only story' received.
South Carolina, Florida and Georgia weeklies reran the wire under 'Negro Shoots Whitecap' and 'White-Cappers in Sumter', still describing Suggs as at the point of death.
The Marietta Journal's one-line brief repeated Cheney's claim that Suggs 'was with a mob which attacked his home'.
A Vermont editorial, its opening lost, told the case as one of a whipping party that came away with 'three badly wounded comrades' while 'the negro's door was still on its hinges'.
